title: Geometry without end
hookLine: stars and interlacing patterns that seem to go on forever

cards: A compass, the kind with a sharp point and a pencil, from a school pencil case. One circle on a blank page. That's all you start with.

From that one circle, with no other tool but a straight edge, craftsmen in Muslim lands drew stars of six and eight and twelve points, bands that weave over and under one another, tiles that lock together and repeat across whole walls and ceilings.
Stand in front of one of those walls and your eye can't find where the pattern starts. Today: geometry without end.

teach.b: These patterns begin with a circle. Open a compass, draw a circle, and without changing the compass, step its point around the edge. It fits exactly six times.
Join those points and a six-pointed star appears. Divide the circle another way and you get eight points, or more.
From those divisions craftsmen built a grid of lines, and from the grid, stars and polygons.
Then they turned the lines into bands and wove them, over, under, over, until the whole surface is one interlacing knot. The Persian name for such patterns is girih, usually rendered a knot.
Now the trick that makes them seem endless. The pattern is built as a repeating unit, a tile that fits against copies of itself on every side.

teach.h: CUT OFF BY THE WALL, NOT ENDED.
teach.b: So when the wall ends, the pattern doesn't; the edge of the building simply cuts it off. Your eye knows it could go on, past the corner, past the city, forever. What does it mean?
The patterns themselves don't say, and Muslims read them in more than one way. Some see the oneness of God: every star, however far out, grows from the same center. Others see the order of creation.

The Qur'an invites the reader to look at the heavens God made, to look again and find no flaw, and says that if the sea were ink for the words of God, the sea would run dry before the words did. Others simply see beauty.
Every reading meets the same thing: patterns without end.

how: Craftsmen in the Islamic tradition draw geometric patterns with compass and straight edge from a single circle, and set them in tile, wood, plaster and stone across mosques, schools and homes.

games.q: you're a craftsman with a compass and one circle. you want a star. what do you do first?
o: step the compass round the circle's edge and mark it.
trace a star from a book.
games.why: keep the compass at the same opening that drew the circle and step it round the edge. it fits six times. join the marks and the star appears.

practice: Draw a circle with a compass, or trace around a cup and mark half its width on a strip of paper to step with. Keeping that same opening, step around the edge from mark to mark until you're back where you began.
Join every other mark into a triangle, then the rest into a second triangle, one slow line per breath, and a six-pointed star appears.

wordCard.voice: Girih. The Persian name for the woven, knotted patterns drawn from a single circle, cut off by the wall but never finished. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: geometry, the measured art behind the patterns.

carryVoice: Your line: patterns without end. The wall stops; the pattern is only cut off. See you tomorrow.
